newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST-British business press - Dec 3.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-British business press - Dec 3.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- FUNDS ATTACK 50 MILLION STG WICKES PLAN

The risk of a possible revolt by institutional investors is increasing over a rescue rights issue at the do-it-yourself retailer, Wickes, where former senior management are under investigation by the Serious Fraud Office. Some fund managers are unhappy that Wickes has increased the amount it plans to raise in a rights issue by 20 million stg to about 50 million stg. Institutions are also uncertain about backing the Wickes directors.
-- TWO MORE LENDERS LIFT MORTGAGE RATES

Northern Rock and Coventry building societies have followed Abbey National and Nationwide by putting up their mortgage rates. Northern Rock is increasing mortgage rates for its 280,000 borrowers from January the second by half a percentage point. Coventry's new rates will be effective from January 1 for its 70,000 borrowers on variable rates and will be 0.26 of a point higher.
-- ELECTRICITY WATCHDOG PUTS OFF COMPETITION

Stephen Littlechild, the electricity regulator, has delayed the introduction of full competition due to pressure from the regional electricity companies. It will mean that only 10 per cent of the country's domestic electricity customers will be able to shop around for their power in April 1998. The move comes after fears that the companies' untested computer systems would collapse, causing chaos for consumers if all 23 million customers were allowed to change supplier on April 1 1998.
THE TIMES
-- EXPORTERS SQUEEZED AS POUND HITS THREE-YEAR HIGH

Sterling has jumped to its highest level against the mark for three years. This comes as evidence emerges that British manufacturers are beginning to suffer from the pound's strength. The latest purchasing managers' survey from the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply reports that the pound is starting to affect exports negatively. The survey showed manufacturing industry expanding for the sixth month running, but recovery remains slow.
-- RACAL SHARES IN 150 MILLION STG SLIDE AFTER WARNING

One of the biggest single-day declines of a top Stock Exchange company has been triggered by a profits warning from the defence electronics and communications group Racal. The shares fell by 18 per cent, wiping 150 million stg off Racal's market value. City analysts warn that the worst may not be over. Racal said it did not know the full extent of the downturn until a board meeting last Friday.
-- LINES FOUND GUILTY OF LYING TO INVESTORS

At the conclusion of a five month trial at the Old Bailey, Richard Lines, former chairman and founder of MTM, the chemicals group now known as Meristem, has been convicted on three counts of false accounting and lying to investors. Thomas Baxter, his former finance director, was convicted on two counts, but acquitted on a third. The collapse of MTM's share price in March 1992 saw losses of 250 million stg for investors, including pension funds and City institutions.
THE GUARDIAN
-- WATCHDOG CASTS FRESH EYE ON CHAT LINES

Telephone regulators have ordered the review of and action against "virtual" chatlines. The inquiry has been triggered by the spate of stories involving huge bills run up by "chat addicts". The Independent Committee for the Supervision of Standards of Telephone Information Services has reports of bills running to 5,000 stg. Concerns have also been raised about adult material discovered on some services.
-- TORIES BACK HEAVIER LORRIES

Transport minister John Watts has said the Government is seeking views on whether to allow six-axle lorries to operate from January 1999. This will mean heavier lorries on the roads and will raise the current limit from 38 to 44 tonnes. Watts claims that 44-tonne six-axle lorries caused less road wear and would carry more goods. The move is likely to receive opposition from transport campaigners and from within the Government itself.
-- DAVIES REJECTS 'PEAK PRACTICE'

Howard Davies, deputy governor of the Bank of England, has rejected proposals which would give the Treasury the leading role in financial supervision in the UK. He described the arguments behind so-called "Peak Practice" concept of regulation where two commissions, one covering systemic risk and the other relations between financial institutions and their retail clients, as "considered and thoughtful". However, he said the upheaval and cost involved may be unwarranted.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- EMAP'S DISSIDENT DIRECTORS VOTED OUT

Shareholders in the media group Emap have voted overwhelmingly to oust Professor Ken Simmonds and Joe Cooke, two "dissident" non-executive directors who had contested charges to the company's articles of association. Emap's chairman, Sir John Hoskyns, and chief executive, Robin Miller, were accused by shareholders of "double standards", "unethical behaviour" and of conducting personal vendettas.
-- SEARS TO RAISE CASH THROUGH FREEMANS SALE

Retail group Sears has confirmed it is in the early stages of talks with several parties to sell Britain's third-largest mail order business, Freemans. The move could pave the way for surplus cash to be returned to long-suffering shareholders. The talks are understood to be with all of Freemans' main rivals in the mail-order business, including Great Universal Stores and Littlewoods.
-- COURTAULDS TEXTILES SELLS LAST SPINNING MILLS

Courtaulds Textiles, the business formed after the Courtaulds empire split its chemicals and clothing businesses in a demerger six years ago, is selling off its last spinning mills in Bolton and Oldham. These are being sold to Shiloh, a long- established quoted textiles and healthcare company based in Oldham. The deal will mark the end of a decline in Courtaulds' yarn spinning businesses.
